EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Climate, Profits, and Productivity in U.S. Agriculture, 1978–2002”

------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-differences–style panel fixed–effects (two-way FE) regression that exploits within-county year-to-year variation in growing-season temperature and precipitation.

Why appropriate?  
•  Weather realizations are plausibly as-good-as-random conditional on location and year, so comparing the same county in hot vs. cool years provides a clean counterfactual.  
•  County FE absorb all time-invariant confounders (soil, distance to market, historical crop mix, political representation, etc.).  
•  Year FE absorb nationwide shocks (input and output prices, macroeconomic conditions, farm-policy changes).  
•  Continuous weather “treatments” allow us to map a dose–response function and then integrate that function with GCM projections to obtain long-run climate damages.

------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variables (continuous):  
T1  Growing-season degree-days (GDD) in four bins, base 46.4 °F, ceiling 89.6 °F  
  DD1 < 50 °F, DD2 = 50–68 °F, DD3 = 68–86 °F, DD4 > 86 °F  
T2  Total April–September precipitation (mm), plus its square to allow a concave response.

Control:  The same county-year observations when the relevant weather variable is at its historical mean. Conceptually, “untreated” is a season with zero incremental degree-days or precipitation relative to the county’s long-run average.

No single event date → not an event study.  
No cutoff → not RDD.

------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
------------------------------------------------------
A1. Within-county exogeneity of weather shocks  
 Plausible: Physical weather is not chosen by farmers and is orthogonal to unobservable profit shocks.

A2. No time-varying confounders correlated with both weather and outcomes after conditioning on year FE (e.g., price × region shocks)  
 Plausibility: Commodity prices are highly integrated nationally; we include year FE and interactions of year FE with USDA Farm Resource Regions to soak up remaining heterogeneity.

A3. Linear additivity/separability of weather effects conditional on FE (i.e., the model is correctly specified)  
 Plausibility: We allow flexible binning, polynomials, and interactions with irrigation share to relax functional-form restrictions.

A4. Short-run weather responses approximate long-run climate responses once we later allow for adaptation (via interactions with irrigation, long-run normals, and decade dummies).  
 Plausibility: Common in the climate-economics literature; we will test sensitivity to adaptation controls.

------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
------------------------------------------------------
T1. Adaptive input changes (e.g., irrigation, crop switching) are endogenous to weather.  
 Fix:  (i) Control for current-year irrigation share; (ii) interact weather with decade indicators to capture gradual adaptation; (iii) estimate separate equations for irrigated vs. non-irrigated counties.

T2. Spatial correlation in weather → underestimated standard errors.  
 Fix:  Cluster by NOAA climate division (≈ 350 clusters) or use Conley (1999) HAC standard errors with a 500 km cut-off.

T3. Measurement error in weather from PRISM down-scaling.  
 Fix:  (i) Average gridded and station data; (ii) instrument county-level weather with upwind station weather using the prevailing jet-stream direction; (iii) show robustness to excluding counties with sparse station coverage.

------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE
------------------------------------------------------
```r
# =========================
# 0.  Libraries
# =========================
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE estimation
library(conleyreg)    # Conley SEs
library(ggplot2)

# =========================
# 1.  Load Data
# =========================
# Assume each CSV in /data
ag  <- fread("data/ag_census_1978_2002.csv")       # Outcomes
wx  <- fread("data/county_weather_1978_2002.csv")  # Degree-days & precip
soil<- fread("data/nri_soil.csv")                  # Soil controls

# =========================
# 2.  Merge & Construct Vars
# =========================
d <- merge(ag, wx, by = c("fips", "year"))
d <- merge(d, soil, by = "fips")

# Bins of degree-days already provided in wx or create here
# Interaction with irrigation share
d[, `:=`(dd1_irrig = dd1 * irr_share,
         dd2_irrig = dd2 * irr_share,
         dd3_irrig = dd3 * irr_share,
         dd4_irrig = dd4 * irr_share)]

# =========================
# 3.  Main Specification
# =========================
fe_formula <- profits_per_acre ~ dd1 + dd2 + dd3 + dd4 +
              precip + I(precip^2) +                                  # quadratic precip
              dd1_irrig + dd2_irrig + dd3_irrig + dd4_irrig |         # adaptation int’s
              fips + factor(year)                                     # two-way FE

est <- feols(fe_formula, data = d, cluster = "climate_division")      # NOAA div cluster
summary(est)

# =========================
# 4.  Robustness: Conley SEs
# =========================
est_conley <- conleyreg(est,
                        lat = d$lat, lon = d$lon,
                        cut.off = 500, cores = 4)
summary(est_conley)

# =========================
# 5.  Robustness: 10-yr normals difference
# =========================
# Calculate 10-year centered normal weather
d[, `:=`(dd4_10yr = dd4 - frollmean(dd4, n = 10, align = "center"),
         precip_10yr = precip - frollmean(precip, n = 10, align = "center")),
  by = fips]

est_rb <- feols(profits_per_acre ~ dd4_10yr + precip_10yr | fips + factor(year),
                data = d, cluster = "climate_division")
summary(est_rb)
```

------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory and prior agronomic evidence imply:
•  Mild additional degree-days below ≈ 68 °F (DD2) should raise yields and profits in cooler counties (positive coefficient).  
•  Heat above ≈ 86 °F (DD4) sharply reduces yields, so expected large negative coefficient.  
Back-of-the-envelope: A uniform +5 °F shift (Hadley-2) is likely to increase damaging DD4 by ~250 °C-days. Given historical elasticities of –$0.50 profit per acre per damaging GDD, expect ≈ $125/acre loss (≈ 20–25 % of 2002 average profits). Land values should capitalize roughly 15× this annual flow, implying 10–15 % decline in land prices in the worst-hit counties.

------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (1 = OK, 0 = concern)
C1 Exogenous treatment assignment……………………………………1  
C2 No time-varying confounders after FE……………………………0.8  
C3 Correct functional form (flexible bins/polynomials)…………1  
C4 Reliable, precise measurement of key variables………………0.7  
C5 Appropriate inference (spatially-robust SEs)…………………1  

Overall score: 4.5 / 5.  

With the outlined design, assumptions are largely credible yet transparent, and multiple robustness checks directly confront the main identification threats.
